text: Eleanor Manning O'Connor (June 27, 1884 – July 12, 1973) was an American architect and educator dedicated to creating decent public housing for all. She was born in 1884 to Delia Josephine Grady and James Manning, a building contractor in Lynn, Massachusetts, whose father, John Manning, was an Irish immigrant and Ellen Horgan's son. Eleanor attended Lynn Classical High School and earned an S.B. degree in architecture from M.I.T. in 1906 with a thesis titled "Design for a Country Residence." She served as president of Cleofan, MIT's club for women, during her senior year. Two years after graduation, she became a draftsman with architect and MIT graduate Lois Lilley Howe. In 1912, she took an extended leave to travel in Europe with her classmate Eliza J. Newkirk Rogers, creating watercolors of the buildings they observed. She returned to accept a partnership with Howe, forming the firm Howe and Manning, which became America's fourth firm of female architects and later evolved into Howe, Manning & Almy, Inc. The firm specialized in remodeling and renovating outdated structures, a practice O'Connor coined as "renovising." In the 1920s, she collaborated with Lois Howe and other architects on the Village of Mariemont in Hamilton County, Ohio. One of her major projects was the Old Harbor Housing Project in South Boston, a WPA commission for low-cost housing in an Irish neighborhood, constructed between 1933 and 1938. This project, developed with the Seventeen Associated Architects, featured three-story apartments and two-story townhouses and was noted for its residential appeal, contrasting with the sterile nature of most public housing. Biographer Doris Cole stated that O'Connor was the partner most focused on social issues, and these concerns were reflected in the project’s detailing, material choices, and attention to proportion. She later served on numerous housing commissions and councils at the city, state, and national levels. After World War I, she began lecturing at Simmons College as a Special Instructor of Architecture and later of Housing, a role she held for 50 years. In the 1930s, she also taught at Pine Manor Junior College, Chamberlain School for Retailing, and Garland College and frequently lectured in the New England area on housing throughout her career. In 1931, she married Johnson O'Connor, an American psychometrician, researcher, and educator, founder of the Johnson O'Connor Research Foundation, where she advocated for women and encouraged their entry into engineering, medicine, and science. O'Connor died in Mexico in 1973 while researching Indian cultures and is buried beside her husband in Newport Beach, California. She was survived by her engineer son, Chadwell O'Connor.
